content:
In our previous Morning Light, we saw that immediately after Israel's failure at Kadesh-barnea, Yahweh gave hope to the next generation. Although the unbelieving generation would perish in the wilderness, He assured their children that they would certainly enter the Promised Land, and He began giving instructions concerning the worship that would take place after they had settled there. Today let us look more closely at the offerings and the measurements mentioned in this chapter. Tomorrow, we will study their spiritual meaning and the lessons they teach the New Creation.

Yahweh instructed Moses that whenever Israel entered the land and presented offerings before Him, certain additional offerings were to accompany the animal sacrifice. These instructions applied whether the offering was presented as a burnt offering, a sacrifice to fulfill a vow, a freewill offering, or one of the appointed festival offerings. The chapter mentions three principal animal offerings. The first was a lamb. The second was a ram. The third was a young bull. Each animal was to be accompanied by a grain offering made of fine flour mixed with olive oil, together with a drink offering of wine. And here we see a beautiful order, for the larger the animal, the larger the accompanying grain and drink offerings had to be.

For a lamb, the worshipper was to bring one-tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with one-fourth of a hin of olive oil, along with a drink offering of one-fourth of a hin of wine. For a ram, the accompanying offering increased. The worshipper brought two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with one-third of a hin of olive oil, along with a drink offering of one-third of a hin of wine. And for a young bull, the largest sacrifice mentioned in this chapter, the accompanying offering increased once again. The worshipper brought three-tenths of an ephah of fine flour mixed with one-half of a hin of olive oil, along with a drink offering of one-half of a hin of wine. So the measurements always increased according to the size of the animal being offered.

The chapter introduces three important units of measurement, and it helps us to understand each one. The first is the ephah. The ephah was the standard Hebrew dry measure used for grain and flour, and its approximate capacity was about twenty-two litres. The ephah was also divided into smaller portions, for Scripture explains in Exodus that one omer is one-tenth of an ephah. Therefore one ephah contained ten omers. Although the omer is not mentioned directly in Numbers 15, it helps us understand the measurements, because the grain offerings are expressed as fractions of an ephah. The second measurement is the hin. The hin was the standard Hebrew liquid measure used for oil and wine, and one hin was approximately three and three-quarter litres. Fractions of a hin; one-fourth, one-third, and one-half; were used according to the size of the accompanying offering.

Another detail worth noticing is the quality of the flour. Yahweh did not ask for ordinary flour, but for fine flour. The Hebrew word is Soleth, referring to flour that had been carefully sifted until it was pure and refined. It represented the finest quality available. The oil mentioned throughout this chapter was olive oil, which was mixed together with the fine flour before being presented. And the drink offering consisted of wine, measured according to the same proportions as the oil, and poured out before Yahweh as part of the offering. Again and again throughout this chapter, Yahweh declares that these offerings were "a pleasing aroma to Yahweh." This expression appears several times in Numbers 15. It does not suggest that God required food or delighted in the physical smell of burning sacrifices. Rather, it signifies that worship offered according to His command was accepted and pleasing to Him.

Yahweh also declared that these same instructions applied not only to native-born Israelites, but also to the foreigners who lived among them. There was to be one law and one ordinance for everyone who approached Him in worship. Then, toward the end of this section, Yahweh introduced another offering that Israel would present after entering Canaan. Whenever they prepared bread from the grain of the land, they were to offer the first portion of their dough to Yahweh as a heave offering. Unlike the grain and drink offerings, no specific quantity was given for this offering. The emphasis was not upon the exact measurement, but upon presenting the first portion of every batch of dough to Yahweh before enjoying the rest themselves.

So Numbers 15 contains a whole list of offerings; burnt offerings, sacrifices offered in fulfillment of vows, freewill offerings, festival offerings, grain offerings made of fine flour mixed with olive oil, drink offerings of wine, and the offering of the first portion of the dough after entering the land. And the most important thing to notice is this: every offering was carefully ordered by Yahweh. Nothing was left to human imagination or personal preference.

Even the measurements were established by His command. This was teaching Israel a precious truth; that worship was to be offered according to His instruction, and not according to human ideas. Tomorrow, God willing, we will look beyond the measurements and the ceremonies to study the spiritual meaning of these offerings, and discover what they teach the New Creation concerning Christ and our worship before the Father.

title: Prayer
text:
O Yahweh, our God,
We see that even the smallest measure of flour and oil was ordered by Your own command.

Nothing in Your worship was left to human imagination or personal preference.

Teach us to worship You according to Your instruction, and never according to our own ideas.

As the offerings grew with the greatness of the sacrifice, let our devotion grow with Your grace.

And may we always bring You the fine, the pure, and the first, for You are worthy of our best.

"Worship Yahweh in the beauty of holiness." - Psalm 96:9

In the name of Christ, we pray. Amen.
